question: A site has two complete, independent power systems (2N), each able to carry the whole load. According to the lesson, what condition decides whether that design actually lowers risk?

options.A: Each system must be sized with one extra spare generator
options.B: The two systems must share no common part, like one switchboard
options.C: Both systems must be load tested together at least once a year
options.D: The two systems must come from two different equipment makers

rationales.A: Adding one spare unit describes an N plus one design. The lesson's point about 2N concerns shared dependencies, so extra spares do not settle it.
rationales.B: Correct. The lesson says two complete systems only help if they genuinely do not depend on anything in common, such as a single switchboard or a single control system.
rationales.C: The lesson does not tie the value of 2N to joint testing. Two systems tested together can still fail together if they share a weak point.
rationales.D: The lesson never mentions equipment makers. Its concern is any shared element, such as one switchboard or one control system.

wrong_choice_note: A is the most tempting because more spare equipment sounds safer. The teaching point is that 2N protects you only when the two systems have no single point in common.
source_excerpt: The difference in risk is subtler, because two complete systems only help if they genuinely do not depend on anything in common, such as a single switchboard or a single control system.

question: Why can't an operator simply run its fleet of emergency backup diesel generators as an everyday power plant when the grid is tight?

options.A: NFPA 110 forbids any standby unit from running past ten seconds
options.B: The UPS batteries must stay charged, which keeps the units offline
options.C: EPA rules cap emergency units near 100 hours a year of routine use
options.D: Uptime Institute certification is voided whenever a unit is started

rationales.A: The ten seconds in NFPA 110 Type 10 is how fast power must be restored. It is a start-up requirement and says nothing about a run-time limit.
rationales.B: The batteries carry the load during the seconds before generators start. They do not stop generators from running.
rationales.C: Correct. Under EPA rules for stationary engines, emergency units are generally limited to about 100 hours a year of non-emergency operation, so everyday use would need different permits and controls.
rationales.D: The lesson links no Uptime certification rule to starting a generator. The limit it describes comes from air regulations.

wrong_choice_note: A is the most tempting because ten seconds is the lesson's most memorable generator number. That figure describes how quickly power must return, while the everyday-use barrier is the EPA hours cap on emergency units.
source_excerpt: Under the Environmental Protection Agency's regulations for stationary engines, generators classified as emergency units are generally limited to about 100 hours a year of non-emergency operation for maintenance and testing.

question: An operator is deciding how much backup to give a hall running a large AI training job. Per the lesson, why might that hall get less redundancy than a payments platform?

options.A: Training hardware draws too little power to justify standby generators
options.B: Training halls are exempt from the Uptime Institute tier definitions
options.C: Payments platforms run on batteries alone, so their needs are smaller
options.D: A job that checkpoints often can restart after an outage, losing only time

rationales.A: The lesson gives no claim that training hardware draws little power. The argument rests on how the workload recovers from an outage.
rationales.B: No exemption is described. The tier definitions apply to whatever is designed, and the lesson treats lighter backup as a design choice.
rationales.C: The lesson says a real-time payments system may justify fault tolerance, which is more protection, so its needs are larger.
rationales.D: Correct. The lesson says a training job that saves progress regularly can often restart from its last checkpoint, costing lost time rather than lost data.

wrong_choice_note: A is the most tempting because AI is often discussed in terms of power draw. The teaching point is that the case for lighter backup comes from recoverability, and it depends on how often checkpoints are saved.
source_excerpt: A large training job that saves its progress regularly can often survive a brief outage by restarting from its last checkpoint, at the cost of lost time rather than lost data.
